entries.test: Copilot subscription prices, usage allowances, and token costs over the three years preceding publication would establish whether users could consume more than their monthly fees.
entries.note: The claim concerns permitted consumption, not necessarily every user's actual consumption.

entries.test: AI services' subscription revenue and compute expenses would show whether every service loses money because it subsidizes compute.
entries.note: The universal claim admits counterexamples.

entries.test: Historical subscription allowances and the compute costs of permitted usage would establish Anthropic's and OpenAI's consumption-to-fee ratios.
entries.note: 'Upwards of $8' includes approximately $8 or above; 'more than $8' imposes a stricter threshold.

entries.test: Comparable task-level inference costs and token consumption across model generations would show whether reasoning-token usage raised inference costs over time.
entries.note: The proposition turns 'prices ... might have come down' into an asserted price decline.

entries.test: Financial results for LLM services would show whether any monthly subscription business is economically sustainable.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives 'economic sense' a plain financial reading.

entries.test: Subscription terms, marketing representations, and service financial results would establish whether the offerings were unsustainable and misrepresented to customers.
entries.note: The normalization drops the substantive accusation that customers were swindled.

entries.test: Reproducible factuality and task-reliability evaluations would establish whether LLMs recurrently hallucinate and fail.
A demonstrably sustainable LLM service that does not bill each user's actual token consumption would refute the claim.
entries.note: It combines a historical assertion with an unlimited future prediction.
The exclusive purpose attributed to the companies is a private motive. The normalization also drops the assertion about how most users perceive benefits.

entries.test: Repeated controlled evaluations would establish variability and unexpected failures in LLM behavior.
entries.note: The surrounding examples concern reliability of task outcomes.
'Really artificial intelligence' supplies no shared criterion for the claimed causal distinction.

entries.test: Published AI subscription billing terms would establish whether a majority move to token-based billing.
entries.note: 'I think it’s inevitable' expresses a firm expectation.

entries.test: If Microsoft becomes financially unable to subsidize compute, other companies' finances and continued subsidies would test whether none can afford it.
entries.note: Changing prices alone would not establish the antecedent.
'Closing time' does not specify which business or industry outcome constitutes the end. The normalization supplies 'the end of the AI boom.'
'I’m not sure' expresses doubt about investment justification under future pricing.
Uncertainty about positive ROI becomes 'probably not,' and 'every study' becomes an unspecified set. The separate universal assertion about studies is checkable.
The estimate is explicitly qualified by 'likely.'

entries.test: Public budget decisions and company reports would show whether cost-conscious businesses struggle to justify five- or six-figure AI spending without demonstrated productivity gains.
entries.note: 'Nobody can seem to measure' does not establish that gains cannot be measured.

entries.test: Investor questions in earnings calls and shareholder communications would show scrutiny of rising AI-related R&D costs when revenue growth fails to follow.

entries.note: The prediction depends on the preceding investor scrutiny and explicitly says 'likely.'

entries.test: Public investor feedback, financing reports, and spending decisions around October 28, 2026 would show whether startups at that spending level struggle to justify it.
entries.note: The six-month horizon has arrived. 'I think ... will' is a firm expectation despite the drafter's 'likely' label.
He expresses uncertainty about hype declining.

entries.test: Project announcements and construction-status records as of publication would establish the announced and under-construction capacity totals.

entries.note: Post-contract earnings are explicitly described as unlikely. The payback-period assertion is separately checkable.

entries.test: Construction pipelines, compute contracts, and customer concentration disclosures would establish the two labs' demand share and exposure to nonpayment.
entries.note: The 50% concentration assertion provides a concrete factual core.

entries.test: Recalculation of the published model's revenue, expenses, depreciation, interest, and amortization would test the stated margins.
entries.note: A hypothetical financial calculation is publicly checkable. Principal repayments and gross-margin accounting require separate treatment.

entries.test: Dated operational reports and construction and equipment cost disclosures would test the building count and estimated total cost.
entries.note: The proposition presents the author's cost estimate as an established project cost.

entries.test: Stargate project financial disclosures and OpenAI payment records would establish how long Oracle takes to earn a profit despite timely payments.
entries.note: 'Even if' strengthens the prediction rather than restricting it to timely payment.

entries.test: Previously announced construction milestones and dated power and operational-capacity reports would establish whether Abilene was behind schedule.
OpenAI's compute obligations, financing, revenue, and cash-flow results through 2030 would test the claimed funding and growth requirements.
entries.note: The normalization omits the annual growth requirement and the requirement to become cash-flow positive.

entries.test: OpenAI's financial results and Oracle payment obligations would establish its losses and the gap between current revenue and required payments.
If OpenAI cannot pay its Stargate bills, Oracle's solvency and continued operation, alongside financing disclosures, would test the prediction.
entries.note: 'Dies' has a plain corporate-failure reading in this financial context.

entries.test: Oracle's available capital, remaining project costs, and partner commitments would establish the funding shortfall under the stated assumption.
entries.note: The source names Abilene, while the proposition substitutes the broader buildout and omits the partner-cost assumption.

entries.test: Stargate customer contracts and financing agreements would establish dependence on OpenAI and whether projected project cash flows entirely support financing and repayment.
entries.note: The normalization drops 'entirely' and the assertion about how the projects are paid for.

entries.test: If Anthropic runs out of money, Google and Amazon's resulting losses and financial condition would establish whether they can absorb the hit.
entries.note: The source firmly says 'can,' while the normalization weakens it to 'could' and adds an explicit Oracle comparison.

entries.test: Anthropic's compute agreements by the end of 2030 would establish whether fulfilling its commitments requires agreeing to annual spending of $25 billion to $100 billion.
entries.note: 'Agree to spend' is changed to actual spending.

entries.test: Recalculating critical IT capacity and rental revenue using the stated PUE and per-megawatt assumptions would test the $156.8 billion estimate.
entries.note: The proposition omits the assumptions on which the revenue requirement depends.

entries.test: Public financial projections and operating economics would establish planned losses over the next few years and whether either company has a financially viable route to profitability.
entries.note: The normalization removes the loss forecast's 'next few years' horizon. Reported financial plans are evidence of planned spending.

entries.test: Compute-provider customer revenues and those customers' financing and cash-flow disclosures would establish how much compute spending depends on continuing debt and venture funding.
entries.note: The firm core is 'a large part'; the majority extension is hedged.
'Nobody can explain to me' becomes a universal judgment about credibility without an agreed standard. The margin comparison is separately checkable.

entries.test: Cursor's January 2026 revenue and cost-of-service figures, including free users, would establish the two gross margins.
AI data centers' utilization, tenancy, cash flows, and depreciation expenses would establish whether operating below 100% necessarily causes the stated losses.
entries.note: A profitable operation below full utilization would supply a counterexample.
The proposition omits payment, tenancy, and depreciation assumptions and changes obsolescence timing. The risk is hedged, although the margin ceiling is separately checkable.

entries.test: Contemporaneous subscription marketing and disclosures compared with documented unit economics would establish whether the services materially misrepresented their economics.
entries.note: The allegation contains a testable misrepresentation claim despite its evaluative language.
The source asserts a present private intention; the proposition substitutes a definite future action.
'Far worse' is an overall judgment of product quality. Specific rate-limit changes are separately checkable.
The explanation attributes a private belief as the cause of customer treatment.

entries.test: Anthropic's release statements, documented deployment capacity, and public technical evidence would test whether capacity constraints rather than exceptional capability prevented release.
entries.note: 'Nothingburger' is a dismissive evaluation, not a precise assertion that the model is ordinary.
This sweeping slogan provides no independent factual test.

entries.test: Published billing arrangements would establish whether LLM subscriptions disappear from code-generating products.
entries.note: 'I truly believe ... are going to' is a firm prediction.

entries.test: Oracle's liquidity and contractual obligations, together with OpenAI's revenue and payments, would test whether exceeding $280 billion in OpenAI revenue is necessary for Oracle's solvency.
entries.note: The financial dependency supplies the testable core.

entries.test: OpenAI's revenue-growth series and scheduled financial obligations would test the slowdown and the claimed tenfold growth requirement by 2030.
entries.note: The source says this precedes a company starting to die; the normalization describes a company already starting to die.
The superlatives function as hyperbolic denunciation in this passage.
Whether outcomes justify a technology's existence is a value judgment. Reliability and financial performance are separately testable.

entries.test: Mathematical analysis of LLM architectures and reproducible demonstrations of novel task solutions would test whether models are restricted to repeating existing actions.
entries.note: The explicit mathematical restriction is a substantive technical assertion.

entries.test: Industry-wide business failures and a sustained collapse in AI investment and commercial activity would establish the predicted industry fall.
entries.note: The financial context supplies a plain industry-collapse reading.
He asks readers to consider a possibility rather than unequivocally predicting insolvency.

entries.test: OpenAI's cumulative revenue and funding through 2030, Stargate payments, Oracle's share price, and disclosed Ellison margin calls and share sales would test the predicted chain.
entries.note: The normalization omits forced share sales and the subsequent further margin calls.
